secondaryCondition: Tendinopathy (fluoroquinolone-associated tendinitis, tendinosis, or tendon rupture)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR 4.71a, DC 5024 (tenosynovitis, tendinitis, tendinosis or tendinopathy), evaluated as degenerative arthritis by limitation of motion under the Note to DCs 5013-5024; a ruptured tendon is separately rateable under the applicable muscle or tendon code in 38 CFR 4.73
primaryCondition: Chronic bacterial prostatitis (service-connected) for which systemic fluoroquinolone therapy was prescribed
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR 4.115b, DC 7525 (prostatitis, urethritis, epididymitis, orchitis (unilateral or bilateral), chronic only)
etiologicalMechanism: SECTION 3.310 DETERMINATION: medication side effect under the treatment-for-a-service-connected-disability route of 38 CFR 3.310(a). The service-connected condition here is chronic bacterial prostatitis, and the fluoroquinolone is the drug class of record for its treatment; the tendon injury is not a second disease arising independently but a direct pharmacological consequence of the therapy prescribed for the service-connected disability. The correct nexus theory is therefore medication side effect, not natural progression of the prostate disease: the prostate infection does not injure a tendon, the antibiotic does, and the claim must be pleaded and decided on that basis. PHARMACOLOGICAL MECHANISM: Fluoroquinolones are bactericidal through inhibition of DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV. Human tenocytes and tendon stem/progenitor cells express topoisomerase II, which is the first step in the toxicity: the drug is not selective for the bacterial enzyme, and it arrests tenocyte proliferation and migration in a dose- and duration-dependent manner, so the tissue loses its capacity to maintain and repair its own matrix. Second, the drugs chelate divalent cations, particularly magnesium and calcium, which are required for integrin-mediated tenocyte adhesion and for normal collagen fibrillogenesis; chelation disrupts the adhesion signalling that keeps the tendon's extracellular matrix under repair, and it also reduces the bioavailability of co-administered cations. Third, fluoroquinolones upregulate matrix metalloproteinases, especially MMP-1 and MMP-13, while down-regulating tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases, producing net collagenolysis of the type I collagen that gives tendon its tensile strength; the same signalling shift increases reactive oxygen species and drives tenocyte apoptosis and premature senescence. Fourth, tendon stem/progenitor cell dysfunction converts an acute injury into failed healing, which is why exposed tendon becomes tendinotic rather than simply inflamed. The anatomical distribution follows the vascular supply: the Achilles tendon's mid-substance, roughly two to six centimetres above the calcaneal insertion, and the rotator cuff are watershed zones with the poorest perfusion, and they are the sites where fluoroquinolone injury concentrates. CLINICAL SIGNATURE AND CHRONOLOGY: symptoms characteristically begin within days to weeks of initiation and can occur without exertion; bilateral Achilles involvement is a recognised hallmark that distinguishes drug-induced from mechanical tendinopathy, and the highest rupture risk is in the first month of exposure. Risk modifiers that a rating decision must document rather than assume are age 60 or older, concomitant systemic corticosteroid use (the combination carries an additive, not merely additive-in-time, risk), renal impairment, transplant status, prior tendinopathy, and male sex. The specificity of the drug-class effect matters for attribution: other antibiotic classes prescribed for the same prostate infection do not carry this boxed-warning risk, so a temporally bounded injury during fluoroquinolone exposure is not explained merely by antibiotic use. Individual nexus reasoning: the examiner should establish the specific agent and dose, the initiation and stop dates from pharmacy records, the temporal relationship of onset to initiation, dechallenge (improvement after discontinuation), rechallenge where it is documented, and imaging or examination localising the injury to a tendon. Competitors to exclude: acute traumatic rupture, gout and pseudogout, inflammatory arthropathy, hypercholesterolaemia and statin exposure, hyperparathyroidism, SLE, local corticosteroid injection, and degenerative tendinopathy that predates the prescription.

medicalEvidence.title: Fluoroquinolones and the risk of tendon injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Alves C, Mendes D, Marques FB
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 15 observational studies. Fluoroquinolone treatment was associated with increased risk of Achilles tendon rupture (OR 2.52, 95% CI 1.81-3.52), Achilles tendinitis (OR 3.95, 95% CI 3.11-5.01) and any tendon disorder (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.62-2.43), with significant estimates persisting in patients aged 60 or older. Effect estimates were not explained away by concomitant corticosteroid use or by study quality, which is what makes this the primary risk anchor; it does not, by itself, establish that an individual's tear was drug-caused.

medicalEvidence.title: Tendon Injury and Fluoroquinolone Use: A Systematic Review
medicalEvidence.authors: Stephenson AL, Wu W, Cortes D, Rochon PA
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of observational studies concluding that exposure to fluoroquinolones is associated with increased risk of tendon injury including tendon rupture and tendinitis, and that risk is elevated in older adults and in corticosteroid users. It establishes the class effect and the risk-modifier pattern the individual nexus must address; being observational, it does not establish causation in a single claimant.

medicalEvidence.title: The Risk of Fluoroquinolone-induced Tendinopathy and Tendon Rupture: What Does The Clinician Need To Know?
medicalEvidence.authors: Kim GK (section editor Del Rosso JQ)
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review of fluoroquinolone-induced tendinopathy written after the FDA-mandated boxed warning, covering the pathophysiology, epidemiology, treatment and outcomes. It is the mechanism anchor for the tenocyte toxicity, cation chelation and matrix degradation pathway, and it records that the tendon injury is a drug-attributable effect rather than a property of the infection; a narrative review cannot grade an individual probability and is used here only for mechanism and regulatory context. Full text: PMC2921747 (PMID 20725547).

secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR 4.118, DC 7827 (erythema multiforme; toxic epidermal necrolysis), rated on recurrence and on impairment of mastication, use of the hands, or ambulation
primaryCondition: Gout (service-connected) for which allopurinol was prescribed
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR 4.71a, DC 5017 (gout), evaluated as degenerative arthritis by limitation of motion under the Note to DCs 5013-5024
etiologicalMechanism: SECTION 3.310 DETERMINATION: medication side effect under the treatment-for-a-service-connected-disability route of 38 CFR 3.310(a). Allopurinol is not treating a service-connected condition incidentally; it is the urate-lowering therapy prescribed for service-connected gout, and the epidermal necrosis is a drug-specific immunological injury to the skin and mucosa. The bone of contention in adjudication is not mechanism but attribution: dozens of drugs can produce Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, and the record must fix allopurinol as the drug of onset. PHARMACOLOGICAL AND IMMUNOLOGICAL MECHANISM: Allopurinol is a purine analogue that inhibits xanthine oxidase; it is metabolised largely to oxypurinol, which is renally cleared and accumulates in kidney impairment, making impaired renal function both a pharmacokinetic amplifier and an independent risk factor for severe reactions. In genetically susceptible individuals, allopurinol and oxypurinol are presented through HLA-B*58:01, and the complex is recognised by drug-specific cytotoxic CD8+ T cells bearing restricted T-cell receptor clonotypes; the drug interacts directly with the T-cell receptor in a peptide-independent, HLA-restricted manner, which is the molecular basis of the allele's strength as a risk marker and of its incomplete predictive value. On activation, these clones deploy a cytotoxic granule-mediating cascade in which 15 kDa granulysin is the principal soluble mediator of keratinocyte death, with perforin and granzyme B, Fas-FasL signalling, tumour necrosis factor alpha, and the IL-15 and caspase pathways acting in concert. The result is extensive keratinocyte apoptosis, full-thickness epidermal detachment with dermo-epidermal separation, and mucosal erosion across the oropharynx, conjunctivae, genitalia and gastrointestinal tract. WHY THE SEQUELAE ARE THE RATEABLE RESIDUUM: acute mortality is high, but for the veteran who survives, the compensable disability is the chronic residuum, because conjunctival and corneal scarring progresses for months to years after the acute event, producing symblepharon, trichiasis, corneal neovascularisation, dry eye and visual loss; genital mucosal disease causes vaginal, urethral and preputial stenosis; cutaneous scarring, dyspigmentation and nail loss may persist; and chronic pulmonary involvement is recognised. Those sequelae arise from the same scarring process that the acute immune injury set in motion, which is why an individual nexus must document the acute event, the drug, and the chronology before rating the residuum under DC 7827. Individual nexus reasoning: the examiner should establish the allopurinol start date and dose from pharmacy records, symptom onset typically within one to eight weeks of initiation, the treating diagnosis recorded at the index hospitalisation, and the continuity of the sequelae from the acute episode forward. Labs during the acute episode are usual; testing for HLA-B*58:01 after the fact supports the drug-specific mechanism but does not substitute for the clinical record, because carriage is neither necessary nor sufficient. Competitors to exclude: other culprit drugs started in the same window (anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, penicillins, cephalosporins, NSAIDs, nevirapine), infection including Mycoplasma pneumoniae and herpes simplex, and other severe cutaneous reactions such as DRESS with which SJS and toxic epidermal necrolysis are commonly confused.

medicalEvidence.title: Severe cutaneous reactions requiring hospitalization in allopurinol initiators: a population-based cohort study
medicalEvidence.authors: Kim SC, Newcomb C, Margolis D, Roy J, Hennessy S
medicalEvidence.summary: Propensity score-matched cohort across five large Medicaid programmes. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions occurred in allopurinol initiators at a crude incidence rate of 0.69 per 1,000 person-years versus 0.04 in non-users (HR 9.68, 95% CI 4.55-20.57); 41 of 45 cases (91.1%) occurred within 180 days of initiation and 12 patients (26.7%) died during hospitalisation. This is the primary anchor for drug attribution, for the initiation-window chronology a nexus letter needs, and for severity; it is a prescribing-population estimate and does not establish causation in an individual claimant. Full text: PMC3502684.

medicalEvidence.title: Strong association between HLA-B*5801 and allopurinol-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in a Thai population
medicalEvidence.authors: Tassaneeyakul W, Jantararoungtong T, Chen P, Lin PY, Tiamkao S, Khunarkornsiri U, Chucherd P, Konyoung P, Vannaprasaht S, Choonhakarn C, Pisuttimarn P, Sangviroon A, Tassaneeyakul W
medicalEvidence.summary: Case-control pharmacogenetic study showing a significantly greater risk of allopurinol-induced SJS/TEN in HLA-B*5801 carriers, with a large effect size reported as an odds ratio. It supplies the drug-specific immunity component of the mechanism and substantiates the allele as a risk marker; the association is ethnic-specific and the allele is not present in all cases, so it is corroborative rather than determinative for an individual.

medicalEvidence.title: Immunopathogenesis and risk factors for allopurinol severe cutaneous adverse reactions
medicalEvidence.authors: Wang CW, Dao RL, Chung WH
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of the immunopathogenesis of allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions, documenting HLA-B*58:01-mediated T-cell receptor interactions with allopurinol and its oxypurinol metabolite, drug-specific T-cell clonotypes with no cross-reactivity to structurally different xanthine oxidase inhibitors, and renal impairment as a determinant of greater severity and mortality. It is the mechanism anchor explaining how a urate-lowering drug kills keratinocytes, and it also identifies the non-cross-reactive alternative therapy a treating clinician can document when the drug must be withdrawn.

secondaryCondition: Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis with painful locking, residual flexion contracture or post-release impairment)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR 4.71a, DC 5024 (tenosynovitis, tendinitis, tendinosis or tendinopathy), evaluated as degenerative arthritis by limitation of motion under the Note to DCs 5013-5024, and, where the index or long finger is functionally impaired, DC 5229
primaryCondition: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (service-connected), with documented duration and glycaemic control
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), with the Note requiring that compensable complications be evaluated separately unless used to support the 100 percent criteria
etiologicalMechanism: SECTION 3.310 DETERMINATION: direct causation. The service-connected diabetes drives a measurable structural change in the hand, and the change is what produces the disability; this is not aggravation of an age-related baseline alone and not a medication effect, although the treatment relationship matters in reverse, because glycaemic control modifies risk. METABOLIC AND BIOMECHANICAL MECHANISM: The flexor mechanism is a tendon travelling through a fibro-osseous tunnel formed by the metacarpal heads and the A1 pulley, a band of retinacular fibrous tissue of the palmar aponeurosis. In sustained hyperglycaemia, glucose forms advanced glycation end products through non-enzymatic glycation and cross-linking of the collagen in both the pulley and the flexor tendons. Cross-linked collagen loses normal sliding and turnover capacity, becomes stiffer, and resists degradation, so mechanical load concentrates instead of being distributed. In parallel, advanced glycation end-product binding to its receptor on fibroblasts and tenocytes activates profibrotic signalling, including transforming growth factor beta and platelet-derived growth factor pathways, which drives fibroblast proliferation, myofibroblast differentiation, and deposition of disorganised matrix; the A1 pulley thickens, and the tendon itself develops fusiform swelling and, in chronic cases, chondroid metaplasia at the point of impingement. Glycosaminoglycan and mucopolysaccharide deposition thickens the retinacular tissue further, the same glycation-driven connective-tissue process that produces diabetic cheiroarthropathy and limited joint mobility elsewhere in the hand. Because the tunnel's cross-sectional area is fixed, thickening of its contents raises the gliding resistance; as the swollen tendon passes the thickened pulley edge it catches, releasing suddenly, which is the audible and palpable triggering that defines the condition, and the catching then produces secondary inflammation, tenosynovial hypertrophy and further narrowing in a self-reinforcing loop. When the process becomes fixed, the digit locks in flexion and the proximal interphalangeal joint may develop a flexion contracture that persists after release. WHY IT MEETS THE AT-LEAST-AS-LIKELY-AS-NOT STANDARD: the causal inference here rests on three mutually reinforcing features rather than on mechanism plausibility alone. First, diabetes is a replicated risk factor, not a co-travelling diagnosis: a population-based cohort of more than 30,000 people followed for over twenty years found diabetes to be the principal independent risk factor for incident trigger finger after adjustment for sex, age, body-mass index, manual work, statin use, smoking and alcohol consumption (adjusted hazard ratio 2.0). Second, the relationship is graded by glycaemic exposure: a nationwide register study of individuals with type 1 and type 2 diabetes found higher HbA1c associated with increased development of trigger finger, which is dose-response evidence rather than a simple association and identifies the exposure variable a treating clinician can document. Third, the anatomy localises the effect to the tunnel, so competing explanations must produce the same focal structure rather than the same symptom. Individual nexus reasoning: the examiner should document the diabetes diagnosis and duration, serial HbA1c values or a control history, the affected digits and their chronology relative to diabetes duration, examination findings of a palpable nodule and reproducible triggering, and, where performed, the operative report showing A1 pulley thickening with or without tenosynovial hypertrophy and the response to release. Competitors to exclude: repetitive or forceful hand use and vibration exposure, rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthropathies, gout and pseudogout, hypothyroidism and acromegaly, amyloid deposition, de Quervain and other tendon entrapments at different tunnels, and preceding local trauma or steroid injection at the same site.

medicalEvidence.title: Diabetes Mellitus as a Risk Factor for Trigger Finger - a Longitudinal Cohort Study Over More Than 20 Years
medicalEvidence.authors: Lofgren JP, Zimmerman M, Dahlin LB, Nilsson PM, Rydberg M
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based cohort drawn from the Malmo Diet and Cancer Study (30,446 individuals) with trigger-finger diagnoses retrieved from the Swedish National Patient Register over more than twenty years. Diabetes at baseline was associated with incident trigger finger with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.0 (95% CI 1.5-2.6) after adjustment for sex, age, body-mass index, manual work, statin use, smoking and alcohol consumption, and remained the principal risk factor. This supplies the temporal ordering and confounding control that an observational cross-sectional study could not; it remains a population-level estimate, not an individual attribution. Full text: PMC10012113.

medicalEvidence.title: High HbA1c Levels Are Associated With Development of Trigger Finger in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes: An Observational Register-Based Study From Sweden
medicalEvidence.authors: Rydberg M, Zimmerman M, Gottsater A, Eeg-Olofsson K, Dahlin LB
medicalEvidence.summary: Register-based study cross-linking the Swedish National Diabetes Register with regional health-care data in 9,682 people with type 1 diabetes and a larger type 2 cohort, testing whether glycaemic control modifies risk. Higher HbA1c was associated with increased development of trigger finger, which is the dose-response element of the nexus: it shows the risk tracks the magnitude of hyperglycaemic exposure rather than merely the presence of the diagnosis, and it identifies documented glycaemic control as the clinical variable the examiner should obtain.

medicalEvidence.title: The impact of diabetes mellitus on tendon pathology: a review
medicalEvidence.authors: Xu J, Wang J, Ji Y, Liu Y, Jiang J, Wang Y, Cui X, Wan Y, Guo B, Yu H
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of the mechanisms by which the diabetic environment damages tendon, covering increased free-radical production and oxidative stress, inflammatory signalling, advanced glycation end-product accumulation and collagen cross-linking, and the resulting alteration of tendon biomechanical properties and histopathology. It is the mechanism anchor for the glycation-driven fibrosis and impaired gliding that produce stenosing tenosynovitis in this population; a narrative review supports the pathway but cannot grade an individual probability. Full text: PMC11575704.

secondaryCondition: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous neuropathy with painful anterolateral thigh dysesthesia, and its residual sensory deficit)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR 4.124a, DC 8529 (external cutaneous nerve of the thigh: anterior and lateral branches), rated 10 percent for severe incomplete or complete paralysis and 0 percent for mild to moderate involvement by the sensory findings recorded
primaryCondition: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (service-connected), with documented diagnostic laboratory criteria and duration of disease
etiologicalMechanism: SECTION 3.310 DETERMINATION: direct causation, as a focal diabetic mononeuropathy rather than a generalised polyneuropathy claim. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a pure sensory branch of the lumbar plexus (L2-L3) whose entire clinical importance flows from its anatomy: it exits the pelvis under the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine and passes through a narrow myofascial tunnel between the inguinal ligament and the iliacus, where it is fixed at both ends and therefore cannot glide when the surrounding tissue changes. Two diabetes-driven processes converge at that point. First, the nerve is metabolically injured by the same hyperglycaemic mechanisms that damage other peripheral nerves: flux through the polyol pathway converts glucose to sorbitol and depletes myo-inositol, non-enzymatic glycation produces advanced glycation end products in the nerve's structural proteins and myelin, oxidative stress injures endoneurial mitochondria, and microvascular disease in the vasa nervorum produces endoneurial hypoxia. The result is a nerve that is already more vulnerable to focal compression than a normal one, with reduced reserves for axonal transport and remyelination. Second, the same glycation process stiffens connective tissue: the inguinal ligament and the surrounding fascia lose compliance, and diabetes is strongly associated with increased body mass index and abdominal adiposity, both of which raise the pressure in the tunnel. The combination produces segmental demyelination with or without axonal loss at the entrapment point, and the clinical result is burning, tingling, numbness or painful dysesthesia in the anterolateral thigh that is characteristically worse with standing, hip extension or prolonged sitting, with no weakness and no reflex change because the nerve is purely sensory. This anatomy-based discrimination is what makes the claim decidable in an individual: an L2 or L3 radiculopathy produces the same distribution of symptoms but originates in the spine, and the two are distinguished by examination, imaging, and by relief with a diagnostic lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block at the inguinal ligament. WHY IT MEETS THE AT-LEAST-AS-LIKELY-AS-NOT STANDARD: the population anchor is a population-based incidence study of meralgia paresthetica in a defined United States county cohort, which established the incidence, the age distribution, and the association with both diabetes mellitus and obesity, so the exposure-outcome relationship is measured rather than assumed; the anatomic and diagnostic literature independently records diabetes among the recognised causes of entrapment at this tunnel. Together they give temporal plausibility, a defined mechanism at a defined site, and a discriminator (the block) that separates the entrapment from the spinal mimic. Individual nexus reasoning: the examiner should document the diabetes diagnosis and duration with control data, the precise territory of sensory loss, exacerbation by hip extension or standing, normal strength and reflexes, imaging or ultrasound of the nerve where available, and the response to a diagnostic injection. Competitors to exclude: lumbar radiculopathy, compressive causes unrelated to diabetes such as seat-belt or belt pressure, tight clothing, prolonged prone positioning, pelvic or acetabular surgery with hardware, obesity alone as an independent cause, retroperitoneal mass or psoas haematoma, and post-herpetic or other focal neuropathies.

medicalEvidence.title: Meralgia paresthetica: relation to obesity, advanced age, and diabetes mellitus
medicalEvidence.authors: Parisi TJ, Mandrekar J, Dyck PJ, Klein CJ
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, identifying 262 patients with meralgia paresthetica, 262 normal controls and 262 body-mass-index-matched controls across 1990 to 1999. The age- and sex-adjusted incidence was 32.6 per 100,000 patient-years, but in people with diabetes it was 247 per 100,000 patient-years, roughly seven times the general-population occurrence, and 28 percent of patients with meralgia paresthetica had diabetes versus 17 percent of body-mass-index-matched controls. A DIRECTION LIMITATION MUST BE CARRIED OPENLY ON THIS ANCHOR: most patients with meralgia paresthetica developed diabetes AFTER the neuropathy was diagnosed, and patients with meralgia paresthetica were twice as likely to develop diabetes (odds ratio 2, 95% CI 1.3-3.0), so the cohort demonstrates a bidirectional metabolic association rather than one-way diabetic causation. An individual nexus therefore has to establish that the service-connected diabetes predated the neuropathy and that no competing cause explains the entrapment; this study supplies the incidence context and the magnitude of the association, not the chronology in a single claimant. Full text: PMC3198972.

medicalEvidence.title: Meralgia Paresthetica: Relevance, Diagnosis, and Treatment
medicalEvidence.authors: Scholz C, Hohenhaus M, Pedro MT, Uerschels AK, Dengler NF
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review of meralgia paresthetica establishing that compression or injury of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve produces pain and sensory disturbance in the ventrolateral thigh, and setting out the diagnostic work-up including the distinction from radicular and other causes and the role of local anaesthetic blocks. It is the diagnostic anchor that keeps the mapping specific to the entrapment site rather than to thigh pain generally, and it records the differential the individual nexus must address.

medicalEvidence.title: Meralgia Paresthetica: A Review of the Literature
medicalEvidence.authors: Cheatham SW, Kolber MJ, Salamh PA
medicalEvidence.summary: Literature review of the anatomy, aetiology, evaluation and conservative management of lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment, recording the tunnel at the inguinal ligament as the site of compression and the recognised associations including diabetes and increased body mass. It documents the mechanical half of the mechanism at the specific anatomic site the DC 8529 rating addresses; as a review it cannot establish an individual nexus and is used for anatomy and evaluation rather than for probability.

etiologicalMechanism: SECTION 3.310 DETERMINATION: direct causation by two converging routes that the record must separate, because they carry the same diagnosis but different evidence. ROUTE ONE, MECHANICAL COMPRESSION BY THE GOITER: the recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus that supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid; it ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove, and the left nerve takes a longer intrathoracic course looping under the aortic arch while the right loops under the subclavian artery. An enlarging thyroid gland, particularly a multinodular or substernal goiter, distorts the adjacent anatomy and compresses, stretches or inflames the nerve against the trachea, the cricoid cartilage or a cervical vertebra; the result is neuropraxia with impaired cord mobility that can be unilateral or, less commonly, bilateral. Extralaryngeal branching, present in a substantial minority of nerves, adds a further mechanical vulnerability because a branch can be compressed independently. ROUTE TWO, IATROGENIC INJURY AT THYROIDECTOMY: the definitive treatment of obstructive or compressive nontoxic goiter is resection, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve is at risk through transection, traction, thermal injury from energy devices, ligature entrapment or ischaemia. Reported rates are on the order of a few per cent for temporary palsy and roughly half to two per cent for permanent palsy, and risk rises with substernal extension, thyroiditis, reoperation, and increasing gland size, all of which are features of goiter managed surgically rather than of incidental nodules. CONSEQUENCE AND RESIDUUM: loss of recurrent laryngeal innervation leaves the affected cord immobile in a paramedian position, producing hoarseness, reduced pitch range and vocal fatigue, and, when the glottis cannot close, dysphagia and aspiration with its own downstream risk of aspiration pneumonia; the volume and quality of the voice, the ability to project it, and the safety of swallowing are the compensable effects and they are what DC 6516 and the analogous evaluation address. A nerve that recovers spontaneously usually recovers within months, so persistence is documented rather than assumed and is a function of the mechanism (transection cannot recover, neuropraxia usually does). WHY IT MEETS THE AT-LEAST-AS-LIKELY-AS-NOT STANDARD: the relationship between benign thyroid disease and vocal cord palsy is documented in condition-specific case series rather than inferred, and the surgical route has large multi-institutional incidence data, which together establish that the mechanism is neither speculative nor rare. What an individual claim must supply is the before-and-after: pre-operative and post-operative laryngoscopy. Where the palsy predates surgery, the compression route is the operative theory and pre-operative laryngoscopy is the anchor; where the palsy appears after surgery in a cord that was documented as mobile before, the iatrogenic route is the operative theory and the operative record supplies the mechanism. Competitors to exclude: thyroid malignancy, which must always be excluded first in a structural thyroid abnormality because nerve invasion by carcinoma is the classic cause; endotracheal intubation-related injury; viral neuropathy; cerebrovascular disease affecting the nucleus or the vagus centrally; and idiopathic vocal cord palsy, which remains a diagnosis of exclusion.

medicalEvidence.title: Relationship between vocal cord paralysis and benign thyroid disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Collazo-Clavell ML, Gharib H, Maragos NE
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective series from the Mayo Clinic of cases with concurrent vocal cord paralysis and benign thyroid disease, documenting eight laryngoscopy-confirmed cases including goiters of various sizes, and concluding that vocal cord paralysis can result from benign thyroid disease through compression, stretching or inflammation while noting that paralysis can also be an incidental finding unrelated to the thyroid. It is the anchor for the compressive route in non-malignant thyroid disease, and it supplies the exclusion requirement (malignancy must be ruled out) that an individual nexus must carry on its face.

medicalEvidence.title: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy in benign thyroid disease: can surgery make a difference?
medicalEvidence.authors: Moorthy R, Balfour A, Jeannon JP, Simo R
medicalEvidence.summary: Condition-specific series of patients presenting with recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy and benign multinodular goitre, analysing the mechanisms of pathogenesis and whether thyroid surgery improves the palsy, in a context where paralysis has usually been taken to indicate locally advanced malignancy. It supports the benign compressive mechanism at the level of the specific disease entity and identifies the surgical decision point, while its small size is why the compressive route should not be asserted for a claimant without laryngoscopic and imaging documentation.

medicalEvidence.title: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury After Thyroid Surgery: An Analysis of 11,370 Patients
medicalEvidence.authors: Gunn A, Oyekunle T, Stang M, Kazaure H, Scheri R
medicalEvidence.summary: Multi-institutional analysis from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program thyroidectomy-specific database, in which recurrent laryngeal nerve injury occurred in 6.0 percent of 11,370 patients undergoing lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, with the rate varying significantly by the primary indication. It supplies the incidence anchor for the iatrogenic route and the evidence that the risk is a function of the operation and the gland, which is what allows a post-thyroidectomy deficit to be attributed to the surgery rather than dismissed as coincidental.
